kuakata-buddhist-temples.desc: Kuakata is home to Rakhine people, Buddhists whose ancestors settled this coast generations ago. Their temples in Kuakata town and at Misripara nearby hold large Buddha images and show distinctive Rakhine architecture. Rakhine villages around them have weaving looms and small shops. The temples offer a quiet counterpoint to the beach crowds.
blocks: How to get there
Walk or rickshaw within Kuakata; Misripara is a short motorbike ride away.
Good to know
Remove shoes, dress modestly and ask before photographing monks or worshippers.

glance: 225 km to Patuakhali by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
kuakata-sea-beach.desc: Kuakata faces south over the Bay, so from different points along its shore you can see the sun come up from the sea at dawn and sink into it at dusk. The beach is wide and gently sloping, backed by coconut palms and casuarina groves. Motorbike riders ferry visitors to the best viewpoints east and west. The town has hotels for every budget.
blocks: How to get there
Direct buses from Dhaka via the Padma Bridge (about 6–8 hrs), or launch to Patuakhali then bus.
Good to know
Hire a motorbike for sunrise at the eastern end and sunset at the western end. Swim only near the main beach and in calm conditions; strong currents occur.

kuakata-rash-mela.desc: On the full moon of the Bengali month of Kartik, usually in November, Hindu devotees gather at Kuakata for a holy dip in the sea at sunrise. The night before, prayers and kirtan fill the beach area, and a fair with stalls springs up. People come from across the south. It is one of the biggest crowd days of Kuakata's year.
blocks: Good to know
Hotels fill quickly; book ahead or come the day after.

glance: Varies by fish, approx. 400–1,200 BDT per kg
Dried fish shops and camps around Kuakata
kuakata-shutki.desc: During the dry season, fishing camps near Kuakata spread fish on bamboo racks to dry in the sun and sea breeze. Loitta, chhuri and small prawns are common. Locals cook shutki with lots of onion, garlic and chilli into a pungent bhuna. Dried fish shops in town let you take some home.

glance: Approx. 100–600 BDT per item depending on size
Evening fry stalls along the Kuakata beach road
kuakata-seafood-fry.desc: Along Kuakata's beach road, evening stalls lay out the day's catch on ice: crabs, prawns, pomfret, squid and more. You choose your piece, it is marinated in spice and deep-fried while you wait. Eaten hot with onion and lemon by the sea, it is a must for visitors. Check the price per piece before ordering.

gangamati-forest.desc: Gangamati lies at the eastern end of Kuakata's beach, where a belt of coastal forest meets the sand. Tree roots and stumps exposed by erosion stand along the shoreline. Visitors come before dawn to watch the sun rise over open water. Fishing boats often work just offshore.
blocks: How to get there
Motorbike or van along the beach from Kuakata, about 30 minutes.
Good to know
Leave around 5 am in winter to catch sunrise; check the tide before riding along the sand.

glance: 225 km to Patuakhali by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
jahajmara-beach.desc: Jahajmara lies in Moudubi union of Rangabali, about 20 km south of the upazila centre and roughly 30 km east of Kuakata. Locals say a foreign ship ran aground here in the British period and slowly sank into the mud; its wreck was visible for years, and the name means 'struck ship'. The beach runs for several kilometres, and both sunrise and sunset can be watched from the sand. Behind it grows a forest of keora, soila and gewa, and migratory birds arrive in winter. Facilities are minimal, which is the point for most who make the trip.
blocks: How to get there
From Patuakhali or Galachipa, travel to Rangabali (road and river crossing), then by motorbike towards Moudubi and Jahajmara; local guides can arrange the trip.
Good to know
Carry food and water and plan to return before dark. Avoid the trip during storm signals or rough-sea warnings.

glance: Bazars and roadside stalls in Patuakhali town and Rangabali, in spring and early summer
patuakhali-watermelon.desc: In the dry months the coastal fields and chars of Patuakhali turn into watermelon beds. The district grew nearly two-fifths of the country's watermelons in 2021–22, and land in Rangabali that once lay fallow now produces big, sweet red-fleshed fruit. In season the fruit is sent all over the country, and local bazars are piled high.

glance: About 100 BDT for visitors, 20 BDT for Patuakhali residents, 10 BDT for students (2023 figures)
winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
kuakata-water-museum.desc: ActionAid set up this museum in Kalapara in 2014 to show how life in Bangladesh depends on rivers. Shelves hold water samples from many rivers, including the ones that cross the border, alongside maps, photographs of rivers that have died, and old fishing tools, brass and clay pots. Panels explain the shared-river problem with India and Myanmar and the 'Kuakata Declaration' on river rights. There is also a small library of books and documentaries. Few Kuakata visitors know it exists, even though it sits beside the main road.
blocks: How to get there
It is beside the Dhaka–Kuakata highway in Kalapara upazila; stop on the way into Kuakata or take an auto from there.
Good to know
Open 10 am–6 pm, closed on Sundays (check, as timings can change). A good stop on a rainy day.

glance: 225 km to Patuakhali by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
majidbaria-shahi-mosque.desc: The mosque was built in the 1460s–70s, under Sultan Ruknuddin Barbak Shah, by his minister Khan-i-Azam Uzayr Khan. After cyclones and pirate raids in the late 16th century the area emptied and the forest took it back. British officials rediscovered the building in the 1860s and had it repaired in 1904. The village name Majidbaria is believed to come from 'masjidbari', the house of the mosque. A large pond with a paved ghat lies beside it, and it is still used for prayers under the Department of Archaeology's protection.
blocks: How to get there
From Patuakhali town go by bus or auto to Mirzaganj upazila, then take a local auto or van to Majidbaria village.
Good to know
It is an active mosque: dress modestly and avoid prayer times.

rakhine-weaving.desc: In Rakhine villages around Kuakata and Kalapara, women weave on looms set up in their homes. The cloth uses bold colours and geometric patterns distinctive to their community. Shawls, sarongs and bags are sold in small shops in Kuakata. Buying directly supports a small community that has kept its culture for generations.
blocks: Good to know
Rakhine-run shops in Kuakata sell directly; ask before photographing weavers.

glance: 225 km to Patuakhali by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
sonar-char.desc: Sonar Char is a char island in Rangabali upazila, in the estuary south of Patuakhali. It has a long beach, mangrove and other planted forest, and is protected as a wildlife sanctuary. Red crabs, migratory birds and deer are among its attractions. Visitor facilities are minimal, so it suits those who enjoy rough travel.
blocks: How to get there
From Patuakhali, travel to Galachipa or Rangabali and hire a trawler; trips are easier with local operators.
Good to know
Go only in calm winter weather with a reliable boat and life jackets; carry water and food.
